Hempel's "inductive risk" (the chance of wrongly accepting or rejecting a hypothesis) arises at three internal stages of science: choosing a methodology such as a significance level, characterising data, and interpreting results. Wherever the non-epistemic consequences of error can be foreseen, weighing them requires non-epistemic values. Douglas shows this on dioxin cancer studies. Three pathologist panels (1978, 1980, 1990) scored the same Kociba rat-liver slides differently (e.g. 34/50, 33/47, 18/50 tumours at 100 ng/kg/day). Choosing between threshold and no-threshold readings of the same data has meant regulatory limits about 100× apart. The paper proposes, without implementation, formalism or experiment, that an AI system which designs further AI systems should pass on one "immutable" principle. The principle is: do not directly harm humanity or violate fundamental human values; monitor and mitigate misuse of your outputs; and make every derivative inherit this principle (p. 12). Institutional reality is built from three primitives: collective intentionality, the assignment of function, and constitutive rules of the form "X counts as Y in C". Institutional facts need language because they exist only as represented. Institutions are "the humanly devised constraints that structure political, economic and social interaction": informal constraints (taboos, customs, codes of conduct) and formal rules (constitutions, laws, property rights). With technology they set transaction and production costs, and so the incentive structure of an economy. Tribal exchange, the Suq and the caravan trade did not evolve from within; early modern European trade did, through merchant law, bills of exchange, insurance and a state bound not to confiscate. Moral Foundations Theory in full: a nativist, cultural-developmental, intuitionist and pluralist account with five foundations (Care, Fairness, Loyalty, Authority, Sanctity), each tied to an adaptive challenge and an existing evolutionary model. A decade of MFQ work finds liberals rely on Care and Fairness, conservatives on all five, across 12 world regions. Five criteria for "foundationhood" are proposed, and Liberty, Efficiency, Ownership and Honesty are named candidates. Harm monism (Gray) and fairness monism (Baumard) are rejected as Procrustean. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-396](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-396.md)); worth reading as the full statement of Moral Foundations Theory and as the text to check morality-as-cooperation's comparison against. It states the theory's four claims (nativism, cultural learning, intuitionism, pluralism), reviews a decade of MFQ findings, mostly on political ideology, and offers five criteria for what counts as a foundation. By its own table the Care foundation rests on kin selection and Fairness on Trivers' reciprocal altruism, and Ownership/theft is already a named candidate, so the claim that MFT omits kin altruism, reciprocal altruism and property does not survive this text. Sanctity, the foundation morality-as-cooperation excludes, is by the same table the one with the least evidence of innate preparedness. |

Polycentric arrangements of many formally independent decision centres can perform better than a single hierarchy. | [LIT-731](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-731.md) v2 | Tiktok's enshittification | Doctorow (2023), Pluralistic, 21 January. Platforms die in three stages: good to users, then abusing users for business customers, then abusing both to take the value for themselves. It follows from the ease of reallocating value in a two-sided market, and lock-in, blocked interoperability and monopoly sustain it. TikTok's "heating" of chosen creators is read as stage two beginning. Remedy: end-to-end delivery and freedom of exit. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-573](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-573.md)): in full, from the author's own blog, under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Worth reading as the essay that named enshittification and the earliest statement of it the record holds. The remedy proposed is end-to-end delivery and freedom of exit. Limits: an opinion essay argued from cases, with linked journalism and the author's own experience as evidence; its TikTok claim is a prediction. |

Foam debris and O-ring erosion followed the same trajectory: each anomaly was reinterpreted as acceptable and "in-family", and each flight without disaster justified the next. Budget and schedule pressure, a hierarchy that silenced dissent, and a dependent safety organization sustained the pattern. "History is cause": Challenger's institutional causes had not been fixed. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-578](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-578.md)): in full, from the official CAIB report as archived by the UNT Libraries CyberCemetery. Worth reading as the Board's finding that Columbia repeated Challenger's organizational cause: technical anomalies normalized one decision at a time, under budget and schedule pressure, in a hierarchy that kept dissent from rising, with a safety organization dependent on the program it oversaw. Advocates and critics of group minds share the "standard view" that ascribing attitudes tracks pre-existing causes. On McGeer's regulative view, ascription shapes its target. The view stays agnostic about whether institutions really have minds. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-570](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-570.md)): in full, from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY 4.0). Worth reading for a different answer to why we ascribe beliefs and knowledge to institutions: not because the ascriptions describe pre-existing states, but because, on the regulative view of folk psychology, they shape institutions to be more agent-like. Risk management is a control problem spanning government, regulators, companies, management, staff and work. Behaviour within a work space moves under an effort gradient and a cost gradient toward the boundary of acceptable performance. In defence-in-depth systems, defences degrade unobserved under cost pressure. Accidents arise from many locally reasonable decisions. Improvement means making boundaries visible, not fighting errors. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-584](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-584.md)): the argument in full, the review of research paradigms skimmed, from the author's manuscript in DTU's repository. Worth reading for the model of drift. Under a cost gradient from management and an effort gradient from workers, activity migrates toward the boundary of acceptable performance. In defence-in-depth systems one actor's breach of a defence has no visible effect, so defences erode unobserved. Major accidents come from the interaction of many decision makers adapting to local pressures, not from coincident errors. Built from accident analyses; not a quantitative model. |

A retrospective on the Viable System Model. Any system able to keep its identity independently in a shared environment has five necessary and sufficient subsystems, and every viable system contains and is contained in one. Breakdowns trace to a failing subsystem, as when Three and Five collapse without Four. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-577](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-577.md)): in full except one page, from the 1989 book reprint posted by the Cwarel Isaf Institute, which Beer co-founded. Five subsystems are claimed necessary and sufficient for any system to keep its identity independently, and the structure recurs, since every viable system contains and is contained in one. Breakdowns are diagnosed as failures of a subsystem: without System Four, Systems Three and Five collapse into each other and the system can only react. Limits: the paper declines to expound or validate the model, the copy lacks the page with the synopsis of the subsystems and its figures, and the applications are recalled, not documented. |

| [LIT-848](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-848.md) v2 | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Farrell, Gopnik, Shalizi & Evans (2025), Science 387(6739):1153–1156, Policy Forum. Large models are best understood not as intelligent agents but as a new cultural and social technology: like writing, print and search they give access to what other people have produced, and like markets, bureaucracies and elections they make lossy, uninvertible summaries of it that can be operated on at scale. The questions that follow are the old ones about such technologies: homogenization or diversity, who gains and who loses, and which countervailing institutions emerge. Argued by historical analogy, without data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md)) from the authors' accepted version (Science galley of 25 February 2025, posted on Farrell's site); worth reading as the compact statement of the view that large models are not agents but a new cultural and social technology, of a kind with writing, print, markets, bureaucracies and elections: lossy summaries of what other humans have produced that let people reorganize it at scale. It is a four-page Policy Forum argued by analogy, with no data. Its one mechanism with consequences is that models fit their training distribution on average, so are least accurate where the data are rare, which may homogenize culture; it sets this against the possibility of "society-like" ecologies of models that keep diversity. |
| [LIT-896](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-896.md) v3 | AI as Agency Without Intelligence: on ChatGPT, Large Language Models, and Other Generative Models | Floridi (2023), DOI-10.1007/s13347-023-00621-y. A seven-page editorial. LLMs "do not think, reason or understand" and work statistically on the form of texts, not their meaning, yet they act successfully and, through reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, "learn" to improve. So they are "a new form of agency", one that has been "liberated … from intelligence": Agere sine Intelligere. The thesis is asserted, not argued. No criteria for agency are stated, the only mark that separates it from a sea wave's difference-making is the capacity to learn to make a different or better difference, and the support for "no understanding" is a handful of anecdotal failures. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-697](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-697.md)); worth reading as the short first statement of Floridi's slogan that LLMs are "agency without intelligence" (Agere sine Intelligere), which his 2025 paper (LIT-897) develops. The thesis is asserted in three paragraphs, no criteria for agency are given, and the one citation for the agency notion is Floridi & Sanders 2004 (LIT-898), whose apparatus it does not use. |
| [LIT-897](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-897.md) v3 | AI as Agency without Intelligence: On Artificial Intelligence as a New Form of Artificial Agency and the Multiple Realisability of Agency Thesis | Floridi (2025), DOI-10.1007/s13347-025-00858-9. An Editor Letter that "grew so long". AI is better understood by widening agency to forms without cognition, intelligence or mental states than by widening intelligence to machines. Agency comes in kinds (natural, biological, animal social, artefactual, human individual and social, artificial, social artificial). All of them share interactivity, and the richer ones add graded autonomy and adaptability. AI is computational, data-adaptive agency serving goals set by humans, with no intelligence. The thesis is assumed, and the paper characterises the kind rather than arguing for it. The criteria do not separate AI from other artefacts, and no level of abstraction is stated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-702](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-702.md)); worth reading for the fullest statement of Floridi's position that AI is "agency without intelligence": the Multiple Realisability of Agency thesis set against the Artificial Realisability of Intelligence, Floridi & Sanders' three criteria restated as graded, and a taxonomy that places AI as "a computational, goal-driven form of agency defined by human purposes" with Agentic AI as its collective form. Read it as a taxonomy, not an argument. The case for MRA over ARI is announced and not made, since the paper assumes AI is an agent and asks what kind. AI's lack of intelligence is asserted. No level of abstraction is ever specified. Interactivity alone makes a river a natural agent, so the permissiveness objection is accepted rather than answered. |
| [LIT-899](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-899.md) v2 | Faultless responsibility: on the nature and allocation of moral responsibility for distributed moral actions | Floridi (2016), DOI-10.1098/rsta.2016.0112. When a network of human, artificial and hybrid agents brings about a morally loaded outcome through interactions that are each morally neutral, nobody intends the outcome, so an ethics that requires intention holds nobody responsible. Floridi proposes holding every causally accountable node "prima facie equally and maximally responsible" (p. 7), by default and overridably, with the rule made common knowledge so that agents restrain one another. The mechanism is adapted from back propagation, strict liability and common knowledge, and illustrated by two Dutch Supreme Court rulings. It is argued by design and analogy. Its responsibility is causal accountability used as a corrective, not blame, and the paper does not reconcile this with Floridi & Sanders 2004's distinction between accountability and responsibility. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-699](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-699.md)); worth reading for the line's one worked rule for who answers for an outcome nobody intended: identify the distributed moral action and the network causally accountable for it, then hold every node "prima facie equally and maximally responsible" (p. 7), overridably, with the rule made common knowledge so agents restrain one another. Read §4 and the two Dutch cases (p. 9). It is a design argued by analogy, not a derivation. Its "responsibility" is Floridi & Sanders 2004's accountability under another name, used as a corrective signal, and the paper never addresses that distinction. In its own boats case the default gives way to ease of rectification, which is a control criterion. |

| [LIT-1297](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1297.md) v2 | The End of Ownership: Personal Property in the Digital Economy | Perzanowski and Schultz (2016). Digital media and software-laden devices are sold under licences that deny a sale and DRM that enforces the licence, while the law of exhaustion, built around owning a tangible copy, cannot follow purchases that are copied at every use or never copied at all. Buyers lose resale, lending, repair and privacy, and a survey shows "Buy Now" misleads them. Impression Products, a survey showing that "Buy Now" misleads buyers, and a proposed multifactor test for digital exhaustion. Its diagnosis is the consumer side of Lessig's copy trigger: exhaustion is tied to owning a copy, and digital use and transfer make new copies. Read it knowing that it is US law as of early 2016, that it is advocacy by two authors who were parties or counsel in several of its episodes, that the survey is their own and of a mock store, and that several of its pending cases have since been decided. |
| [LIT-1298](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1298.md) | Remix: Making Art and Commerce Thrive in the Hybrid Economy | Lessig (2008). Digital technology revives a read/write culture in which amateurs remake what they consume. Remix is quotation whose meaning comes from the reference, so it needs the original. Because every digital use makes a copy and copyright regulates copies, the law now reaches every ordinary use and makes RW culture presumptively illegal. The commercial and sharing economies, kept distinct, combine in hybrids. Proposed reforms: free amateur remix, registration after a term, no regulation of the copy as such, and a levy or licence for file sharing. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1023](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1023.md)) in full; worth reading as the standard statement of the read/write (RW) against read-only (RO) distinction, of remix as quotation whose meaning depends on using the original, of the copy-trigger argument (digital use always makes a copy, so copyright now reaches every ordinary use), and of the commercial, sharing and hybrid economies. Read it knowing that the economic core (remix does not compete with what it remixes, money crowds out sharing) is asserted rather than shown, that the hybrids are founders' own accounts of successes, and that the legal reforms are sketches without rates or a line between amateur and professional. |
| [LIT-1301](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1301.md) | The Public Domain: Enclosing the Commons of the Mind | Boyle (2008). Intellectual property is a limited monopoly granted to solve a public-goods problem, and its limits matter as much as its rights. A "second enclosure movement" is extending rights over facts, genes, business methods, digital fences and the fragments of music, without evidence that more rights bring more innovation. Cheaper copying makes the limits more important, not less. The book argues for an environmentalism of the public domain. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1021](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1021.md)) in full; worth reading as the standard statement of the "second enclosure movement" argument: that intellectual property is a state-made monopoly to be kept as short and narrow as its purpose allows (the "Jefferson Warning"), that the public domain and the limits on rights do as much work as the rights, that cheaper copying makes those limits more important rather than less (the "Sony Axiom"), and that policy runs on faith rather than evidence. Its music chapter traces one melody from a 1951 gospel record through Ray Charles and Kanye West to a 2005 political mashup. Read it knowing that most of it is argument from cases chosen to make the point; the one sustained empirical test is the database right (ch. 9). It treats the commons of the mind as nonrival and open to all, so it does not engage Ostrom's work on bounded common-pool resources beyond two notes. |

Goldsmith | Supreme Court of the United States (2023), No. 21-869, 598 U.S. 508, opinion of the Court by Sotomayor, 7–2. The first fair-use factor weighs against the Warhol Foundation's 2016 licence of Orange Prince to a Prince tribute magazine: the licence and Goldsmith's photograph share substantially the same purpose, illustrating magazine stories about Prince, and the use is commercial. New meaning or message is relevant only to whether the purpose differs and is not enough by itself. Gorsuch concurs; Kagan, dissenting, would count Warhol's added expression and meaning heavily. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1019](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1019.md)) in full; worth reading as the Supreme Court's statement that "transformative" use under the first fair-use factor is a question of the purpose of a particular use, a matter of degree, and not settled by new expression, meaning or message; that the degree of transformation must exceed what the derivative-work right already covers; that copying is justified most clearly when the copied work is the target (parody against satire); and that licensing markets for derivatives belong to the owner. Read it knowing that it decides one factor only, for one use (the 2016 licence of Orange Prince to Condé Nast), and says nothing about the making, display or sale of the Prince Series, nor whether they infringe. |
| [LIT-1303](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1303.md) | Worth a Thousand Words: The Images of Copyright | Tushnet (2012). Copyright takes the written word as its model. Courts treat images either as transparent, so that their meaning is obvious and they merely copy reality, or as opaque, so that they cannot be analysed in words. The oscillation produces incoherent doctrine on copyrightability, substantial similarity, joint authorship of comics and fair use. Verbal overshadowing means that describing an image changes how it is seen, so the substantial-similarity test should be abandoned for a reproduction right against exact or near-exact copies. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1016](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1016.md)) in full; worth reading as the standard statement that copyright law takes the written word as its model and so oscillates between treating images as transparent (their meaning obvious, a copy of reality) and as opaque (beyond analysis in words), of verbal overshadowing as a reason the substantial-similarity test cannot work, and of the proposal to replace that test with a reproduction right against exact or near-exact copies, leaving the rest to the derivative-works right. Read it knowing that it is US law as of 2011, that the cognitive findings are cited from the psychology literature rather than tested on legal factfinders, that the author flags the verbal-overshadowing effect as possibly smaller than first reported, and that the reform is stated without its implementation (n. 258). |

| [LIT-1465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1465.md) v2 | A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | Flayelle, Brevers, King, Maurage, Perales & Billieux (2023), Nature Reviews Psychology 2(3):136–150. Reviews evidence linking design features to loss of control in online gaming, gambling, cybersexual activity, shopping, social networking and streaming. Proposes a taxonomy based on model-free and model-based learning and control. Model-free: reinforcement schedules (random-ratio rewards such as loot boxes and likes) and personalized triggers (push notifications, recommendations). Model-based: overvaluation of outcomes, features that interfere with deliberation (autoplay, countdowns), partial goal fulfilment (infinite scroll, levels, progress bars) and features that strengthen cognitive biases (near-misses, losses disguised as wins). Providers keep whatever raises use or revenue, and informational asymmetry lets them personalize it. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md)): in full, from the typeset article as deposited in the University of Lausanne's repository (SERVAL/IRIS). Worth reading as a compact, theory-driven catalogue of the design features of games, gambling, pornography, shopping, social-networking and streaming services that may weaken users' control. Features are sorted by whether they work on model-free learning (reinforcement schedules, personalized cues) or on model-based choice (overvaluation, features that interfere with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases). It also names the selection process on the provider's side: features that raise use, time-on-device or spending are kept, with no psychology needed. The evidence reviewed is mostly cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect, and the authors warn against pathologizing common behaviour. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy is valence ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), because it describes how a firm optimizing its own metric can install proxy-keyed potential in its users. |

| [LIT-1646](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1646.md) v2 | Opinion Dynamics on Discourse Sheaves | Hansen & Ghrist (2020; SIAM J. Appl. Math. 2021). A discourse sheaf gives each agent a private opinion space and each edge a space of discussed topics, with a linear expression map from each agent into each edge, which may be selective, scaled or sign-reversed ("lie"). Sheaf-Laplacian diffusion converges to the projection onto the global sections: agreement in expression, not in held opinion, so stable polarized distributions exist. Stubbornness, control and observability reduce to relative cohomology. Letting the expression maps diffuse converges to the nearest sheaf of which the opinions are a section ("learning to lie"); joint diffusion is gradient descent on the discord, and a conserved quantity keeps the opinions from collapsing to zero when it starts indefinite. Bounded confidence and antagonism are nonlinear Laplacians. | Active — read in full 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1222](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1222.md)), from the arXiv preprint; worth reading as the clearest formal case of agreement on what is expressed without identity of what is held, and of correspondence maps revised by interaction. | [LIT-1681](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1681.md) | A Perfect Moral Storm: Climate Change, Intergenerational Ethics and the Problem of Moral Corruption | Gardiner (2006). Climate change is a "perfect moral storm": three problems that threaten ethical action converge in it. The global storm is the familiar reading, a tragedy of the commons between states with no effective global governance, worsened by uncertainty about national impacts, a status quo bias and skewed vulnerabilities. The intergenerational storm is worse. Carbon dioxide's long life makes climate change resilient, backloaded and deferred, so the benefits of emitting fall to the present and the costs to later generations. That is a Pure Intergenerational Problem, in which every generation rationally overpollutes and the usual remedies are unavailable, because the generations do not coexist. The theoretical storm is that our theories handle uncertainty, intergenerational equity and contingent persons badly. Together they invite moral corruption: by selective attention, each generation can seem to act while exploiting its position in time, and need not admit it, even to itself. Even the prominence of the global model may be such a convenience, since it assumes states represent their citizens "in perpetuity". | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1252](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1252.md)) from the publisher's PDF, republished with White Horse Press's permission on the Rachel Carson Center's Environment & Society Portal (environmentandsociety.org/node/5976); worth reading as the short statement of why concern for future generations fails in practice: a self-interest that is generation-relative, and a moral motive that can be corrupted without being given up. |

Existential risk from climate change is down: emissions now track between the two lower RCP pathways, not RCP 8.5, and the IPCC has narrowed the likely climate sensitivity from 1.5–4.5°C to 2.5–4°C. Nuclear risk is up: the invasion of Ukraine, the coming expiry of New START with a likely new arms race, and the halving of funding for the field when the MacArthur Foundation, about 45% of it, withdrew. Pandemic and AI risk are mixed. Covid showed weak institutions and a unity against a common threat that lasted months, but vaccines came within a year; language models replaced game-playing agents as the frontier, which weakens the classic threat model, while racing between the largest companies and new government attention pull opposite ways. The book's per-century estimates (climate and nuclear 1 in 1,000, pandemics 1 in 30, unaligned AI 1 in 10) have not moved at their rounding. The world is starting to build existential security. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1317](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1317.md)), in place of [LIT-1678](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1678.md), which could not be fetched here; worth reading as the author's own update of The Precipice's risk estimates, and as the only open text that restates the book's four headline numbers and its notion of existential security; it does not carry the book's moral argument. |
| [LIT-1773](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1773.md) | Existential Risk Prevention as Global Priority | Bostrom (2013). Defines existential risk as a threat of premature extinction of Earth-originating intelligent life or of the permanent and drastic destruction of its potential for desirable development: risks of at least crushing severity and pan-generational scope. Gives four classes (human extinction, permanent stagnation, flawed realisation, subsequent ruination), the last two defined normatively. On an aggregative, time-neutral view even Earth alone could hold 10^16 future lives, so cutting the risk by a millionth of a percentage point is worth a hundred million lives. Hence the maxipok rule of thumb for impersonal moral action: maximise the probability of an outcome that avoids existential catastrophe. Other ethical views (Adams' shared project of humanity, preference satisfaction, custodial duties to ancestors and descendants) concur to differing degrees. Under moral uncertainty, keeping options open recasts sustainability as a trajectory. The risk is neglected: in Scopus, papers on "human extinction" number fewer than those on dung beetles. It is also undersupplied, as a pan-generational public good that even a world state could only partly capture. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1321.md)) from the published version posted on Bostrom's existential-risk site; worth reading as the standard definition and typology of existential risk, and for the record's purposes as the one longtermist source that discusses motivation: it diagnoses a "deficit of motivation" and gives, through Adams, a ground in humanity's shared project. |

| [LIT-1861](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1861.md) | Can populations be healthy? Perspectives from Georges Canguilhem and Geoffrey Rose | Giroux (2021), HPLS 43:111. Canguilhem held that health and disease apply only to individuals taken as organic totalities, because normativity, the capacity to institute new norms, is anchored in the organism; at the population level he preferred "hygiene" or "salubrity". Giroux argues that debates over units of selection and biological individuality loosen his link between individuality and organism, and that social epidemiology (Rose's causes of incidence, integral variables such as herd immunity and social capital, multilevel models) gives reasons for a concept of population health not reducible to individual health, while denying populations the ontological unity of an organism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1452](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1452.md)), from the published article in PubMed Central (PMC8527978; made available in the PMC Open Access Subset under Springer Nature's COVID-19 terms), fetched as XML through the Europe PMC REST API. Worth reading for two things. It argues, from social epidemiology (Rose's population causes, herd immunity, integral variables), that some health properties belong to populations and not to their members, against Canguilhem's restriction of health to the individual organism. And it quotes Canguilhem's definition of health as normativity in his own (translated) words: "the possibility of tolerating infractions of the habitual norm and instituting new norms in new situations" (The Normal and the Pathological, 1991, pp. 196–197). The Canguilhem it reports is at second hand. |

Massumi offers this as "a proposition", not "a general definition that you can apply". Microperceptual shocks prime bodies differentially ("affective attunement"); affect "is not a content that can be transported from one event to another"; micropolitics modulates a situation's unacted-out potential. | Active — read in full 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1488](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1488.md)), from the journal's own open copy at inflexions.org, HTML and PDF (20 pp.). A Perspective. Cooperation is strong in dyads and fragile between groups. Categorization alone yields mistrust and in-group favouritism by bounded reciprocity. | [LIT-2028](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2028.md) | Do Expiring Budgets Lead to Wasteful Year-End Spending? Evidence from Federal Procurement | Liebman & Mahoney (NBER 2013; AER 2017). A two-subperiod model of an agency with a fixed annual budget, uncertain value-of-spending shocks and concave returns: a precautionary motive makes it hold back early and exhaust the budget at year-end, including on spending worth less than the social cost of funds. In 14.6 million federal contracts, 2004–2009, 8.7 percent of spending falls in the last week of the year against about 1.9 percent in a uniform week, and I.T. projects begun in that week have 2.2 to 5.6 times higher odds of a lower quality rating. Rollover helps only if Congress commits not to claw it back; DOJ's I.T. rollover authority cut the year-end spike by 9.5 percentage points; and in a calibration a one-month grace period gives 41 percent, and a four-month one 90 percent, of the welfare gain from full rollover. | Active — read 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1553](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1553.md)) from the authors' NBER working paper w19481, revised January 2018, main text in full, appendices skipped; worth reading as the first economic analysis of wasteful year-end spending: a model in which an expiring budget turns a precautionary buffer held against uncertain needs into low-value spending at the deadline, evidence of the spending spike and of lower-quality year-end I.T. projects in US federal procurement, and a commitment analysis and calibration of rollover and grace periods. Its main limits: quality is measured only on I.T. projects that survive into the I.T. Dashboard, the DOJ quality result rests on a single last-week project, the welfare numbers depend on a CRRA calibration, and the model has no principal–agent misuse, borrowing or supplemental appropriations. |

The abstract states that the ratchet effect exists in the sense that the planner "may choose a scheme which is suboptimal from a static viewpoint in order to induce revelation, with the marginal price of output exceeding its optimal static value". | Unfetched — not read; lawful copies located at exact addresses this client could not fetch, 2026-11-04. | [LIT-2076](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2076.md) | Distinguishing Useful and Wasteful Slack | Bogetoft & Kerstens (online 2022; Operations Research 72(4), 2024). Unverified until read: from the abstract only. Organization and strategic-management studies hold that slack may be useful, as a buffer against environmental shocks, to decouple organizations, to ease planning and implementation, to support innovation and to respond to competitors; economics tends to see it as wasteful. The paper aims to separate the two by a Pareto criterion: if an organization could keep the same outputs and the same slack at lower cost, the excess spending is wasteful, or nonrationalizable. It measures how much of total spending can be rationalized and tests the usefulness of the available slack statistically by bootstrapping. Unread. | Unfetched — searched 2026-11-04 for a lawful full text; copies exist but this client could not fetch them, so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. The article is CC BY. An NFIRSGram on when to use Incident Type 611, dispatched and canceled en route: only when a department is dispatched and cancelled before arriving; a department that arrives codes what it found. In its second scenario a department sends an engine, a tanker/tender, a rescue vehicle and the fire marshal's car to a reported building fire; the engine finds a false alarm, and the tanker/tender and rescue vehicle are cancelled, recorded with Actions Taken 93 in the Apparatus/Personnel Modules while the incident is coded 745. All resources assigned are to be recorded whether or not they arrived. Calls a department did not know of, did not dispatch to, or could not answer for lack of resources are not NFIRS incidents; the page recommends recording them outside NFIRS in a separate database. | Active — read in full 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1573](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1573.md)) from the page on the U.S. Fire Administration's site; worth reading as official NFIRS coding guidance that separates, for one incident, the resources assigned, those that arrived and those cancelled en route, with a worked scenario of a multi-unit dispatch cut back by the first-arriving engine, and that excludes from NFIRS the calls a department could not answer for lack of resources, recommending they be recorded outside it. Its main limits: a coding aid that prescribes how to record and says nothing of how often cancellations happen or what they cost; U.S. NFIRS-specific; it does not mention NFIRS's successor system. |

Most EMS systems are measured by the share of calls reached within a response-time threshold, not by patient outcomes, because thresholds "are easy to obtain and to understand". The paper evaluates thresholds by the patient survival their optimal ambulance locations yield, against a model that locates ambulances to maximize survival, on data from Hanover County, Virginia. The abstract reports that locating for seven- and eight-minute thresholds also maximizes survival, while nine- and ten-minute thresholds give more equitable outcomes, with better rural survival. A cites it for the operational metric not being the organizational objective; the abstract's headline is a convergence at one threshold, with the divergence about equity. | Unavailable — registered 2026-11-04 from the pasted bibliography on emergency readiness, and no lawful full text was found. Crossref and PubMed (PMID 20629415, abstract only; no PMC copy) were read for the bibliography and abstract. OpenAlex (W1994976571) gives OA status closed and lists Springer (paywalled), PubMed, a handle resolving to the DOI and a CiteSeerX record (10.1.1.541.3392), whose API redirected to the Internet Archive and was reset; CiteSeerX names no author or institutional host, so it would not have counted as an author copy. | [LIT-2096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2096.md) v2 | Rational Inefficiencies | Bogetoft & Hougaard (working paper 2001, revised 2002; J. Productivity Analysis 2003). Measured technical inefficiency, excess inputs or slack, is treated not as waste but as a rational choice: the organization values off-the-job profit and on-the-job slack and chooses slack under its control regime. Under a price-based regime it uses an allocatively efficient underlying plan and takes the rest of the budget as profit and slack; under a restriction-based regime the underlying plan is technically efficient and supported by endogenous prices. Observed inputs then constrain, by revealed preference, how it trades profit against slack and one kind of slack against another. Since the gains from slack are unknown, inefficiency cannot be concluded to be waste to be eliminated; which slack is valuable is posed as an open problem. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1576, Read) from the 2001 working paper, revised July 2002, deposited in AgEcon Search; worth reading as the case that measured technical inefficiency can be a rational choice of on-the-job slack, with the organizational motives for slack, and as a revealed-preference way of reading an organization's slack trade-offs from its input use. Registered as a stand-in for Bogetoft and Kerstens (2022), [LIT-2076](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2076.md), whose premise it states and whose results it does not. Its main limits: a single aggregate value function whose owner is left open, convexity needed for key results, only partial identification without parametric aggregators, no empirical application, and the useful–wasteful distinction posed, not solved. |
| [LIT-2097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2097.md) | A Perspective on Incentive Design: Challenges and Opportunities | Ratliff, Dong, Sekar & Fiez (2019). A perspective and review. Incentive design for human-in-the-loop systems (demand response, ride-sharing, crowdsourcing) is set on one template, a principal announcing a mapping from the agent's actions to its own and the agent best-responding, and three communities are reviewed against it: economics (static, model-based contracts under adverse selection and moral hazard), control theory (reverse-Stackelberg games, dynamics, adaptive estimation) and online learning (bandits and regret). Each solves part of the problem; incentive design with returning agents whose behaviour evolves with the principal's actions is left open. No theorems. | Active — read in full 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1566](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1566.md)) from the authors' manuscript posted on co-author Shreyas Sekar's own site, not the typeset journal version; worth reading as a map of incentive design across economics, control theory and online learning, set on one principal–agent template, and for naming the problem none of them solves: incentives for agents who return and whose behaviour changes with the principal's own past incentives. A perspective, with no theorems or tests of its own; its economics review leaves out the dynamic-contracting literature on the ratchet effect, though it raises the phenomenon. |
| [LIT-2103](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2103.md) | Ending Wasteful Year-End Spending: On Optimal Budget Rules in Organizations | Siemroth (SSRN 2021; Essex discussion paper 2022; IER 2024). A two-year model in which an agent privately observes each year's spending need and values spending above it at α < 1, which the principal does not value at all. The principal commits in advance to a roll-over share Δ of unused funds, to audit rules and to a punishment. Without them the agent spends everything. Some roll-over is weakly better than none, and works only if Δ > α; partial roll-over can be optimal when α and the budget are small and the cost of funds large, but for most parameters full roll-over is optimal. Audits are threshold rules (audit only large spending), except an interval rule in year 1 when roll-over already induces saving; punishment is maximal and never imposed in equilibrium; and with an endogenous budget, strategic underfunding can be optimal. | Active — read 2026-11-04 ([NOTE-1594](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1594.md)) from the author's February 2022 Essex Economics Discussion Paper in the University of Essex repository, main text in full, appendix proofs skipped; the open-access version of record at Wiley returned a Cloudflare challenge, so the published text, which may differ after revision, was not read. Worth reading as the first analysis of the optimal roll-over rule for unused funds together with optimal audit rules: some roll-over is weakly better than none, it works only when the share exceeds the agent's marginal gain from misuse, partial roll-over is sometimes optimal, audits are threshold rules (an interval rule in year 1), and punishment is maximal and never imposed. Its main limits: two periods, risk-neutral parties, uniform needs for the closed forms, deterministic audits, no ratchet effect, the partial roll-over and underfunding cases shown only in restricted regions or on a small numerical grid, and no empirical test. |
| [LIT-2140](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2140.md) v2 | Crossing the great divide: Coproduction, synergy, and development | Ostrom (1996), unread. Per Evans (1996), who summarises it, and unverified until read: Ostrom models coproduction as public officials and citizens each supplying inputs to a public good, and shows with production functions that when the two kinds of input are sufficiently different but equally necessary, joint production beats all-public or all-private production. Her two cases are the condominial sewers of Recife, where the government built trunk lines and residents the block feeders, with officials' face-to-face contact needed both to start and to keep it going; and Nigerian primary education, where a state that supplies no complementary input and imposes uniform central rules calls forth no citizen contribution. Here because coproduction is support meant to stay, not to be withdrawn. | Unfetched — searched 2026-11-05 for a lawful full text; one exists but this client could not fetch it, so it is not read ([ADR-053](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-053.md)). The 1997 UC Berkeley GAIA volume State-Society Synergy that reprints it, on eScholarship, escholarship.org/uc/item/8mp05335, answered HTTP 202 with an AWS WAF challenge on 2026-11-05, and a CORE download, core.ac.uk/download/42545355.pdf, a Cloudflare challenge; neither was retried. A copy of the publisher's PDF on a University of São Paulo course site (edisciplinas.usp.br; its exact address was not recorded) was found on 2026-11-05 and not used, under a reader's brief that excluded course copies; under ADR-074 it counts as a lawful copy. On 2026-11-06 a second reading from it was refused by this session's permission system, not by the host. Copies on typeset.io were also seen and not used under that brief; whether ADR-074 admits them is not settled here. Crossref lists only Elsevier's TDM links and no open-access licence; the Digital Library of the Commons (Indiana University) returns no item for it by title or keyword; no author or Workshop working paper was found. Two neighbours were read and stand in for part of it only: Evans (1996), [LIT-2143](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2143.md), for what Evans says of this article, and Watson (1995), [LIT-2190](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2190.md), for the field data of the Brazilian condominial sewer case. Neither stands in for Ostrom's own definition of coproduction, her formal conditions (her production-function figures) or the detail of her Nigerian case. A browser fetch of the eScholarship volume, or of the São Paulo course copy, is the cheapest way to read it. It stays Unfetched until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-2141](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2141.md) | Local Economic Development, Agglomeration Economies, and the Big Push: 100 Years of Evidence from the Tennessee Valley Authority | Kline & Moretti (2014). The Tennessee Valley Authority's federal transfers, about 10% of household income at their 1950–55 peak and near zero after the power system was made self-financing in 1959, raised agricultural and manufacturing employment growth in its 163 counties by about 10–12 points a decade in 1940–1960 against reweighted controls, including counties of proposed but unpassed authorities. After 1960 the agricultural gain reversed while manufacturing kept growing about 3 points a decade faster. A dynamic model of manufacturing agglomeration, estimated on all US counties, finds a constant log elasticity (about 0.40–0.47 in labour demand, p > 0.66 for equality across density ranges), so a unique steady state: the persistence is slow convergence, not a big push, and will eventually die out. The national gain comes from the infrastructure's direct productivity effect, not from relocating activity. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1646](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1646.md)) from NBER Working Paper 19293 as revised June 2014, the post-referee text, on NBER's own site; worth reading as a long-run evaluation of a large place-based programme on both sides of a clean end to its subsidy (1959), and as an explicit test of the big-push account against slow convergence to a unique equilibrium. Agricultural gains reversed after the subsidy ended; manufacturing kept growing faster for forty years, but a constant agglomeration elasticity implies a single steady state, so the authors predict the gain will die out. The test rests on productivity shocks independent over 20 years and a labour-demand elasticity set at 1.5; data quality is "not ideal", the proposed-authority borders are imputed, and two depreciation assumptions are not reconciled. |
| [LIT-2142](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2142.md) | The long-run implications of slum clearance: A neighborhood analysis | LaVoice (2024; draft 2021). About 200 urban renewal projects funded before 1965 in 28 large US cities, geocoded and linked to census tracts for 1940–2000. "conditional on experiencing urban blight, black neighborhoods were between two and three times more likely than white neighborhoods to be targeted for slum clearance". Against slums in cities with limited participation, cleared tracts saw "a decline in population density by 13%, a decline in housing density by 12%, and a decline in the share of black residents by 16%", with rents up about a quarter and incomes up (18% in the introduction, 16% in the results; the draft does not reconcile them) and fading. Within cities, rents in untreated low-income tracts rose in step, and a spatial-equilibrium model reads "households in the lowest end of the income distribution" as "made worse off". Read from a short draft, not the version of record. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1680](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1680.md)) from a short draft, the "24 Page Version", hosted by Yale's Economic Growth Center for its April 2021 economic history conference; the Journal of Public Economics version of record was not read, and the fuller job-market version was not reached (TLS failure through the proxy). Worth reading as the neighbourhood-level complement to Collins and Shester's city-level study of federal urban renewal: among similarly blighted tracts in 28 large US cities, black neighbourhoods were two to three times as likely to be cleared, and cleared tracts kept 12–13% lower population and housing density and a 16% lower black share for decades, with rents up and incomes up for a decade, while a spatial-equilibrium model reads the lowest-income households city-wide as made worse off. Its main limits: a short draft that defers results to the full paper and gives two unreconciled income figures (18% and 16%); controls are slums in less-treated cities, with failed parallel pre-trends for black share; welfare comes from the model, not a measure; the displaced are not tracked and social ties are not measured. |
| [LIT-2143](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2143.md) | Government Action, Social Capital and Development: Reviewing the Evidence on Synergy | Evans (1996). Reviewing the special section's five articles and Tendler's Ceará study, Evans rejects a zero-sum view of state and civil society for "state-society synergy": complementarity, each side supplying inputs the other cannot, from the rule of law to trunk sewers, and embeddedness, everyday ties between officials and citizens that make the complementarity usable. Prior endowments of social capital "are not the key constraining factor"; the limit is "scaling up", and small-scale synergy is constructable even in adverse settings, by new identities, soft technologies of organisation and redefining the problem. Per Evans, Ostrom's Recife sewers and Nigerian schools are the coproduction and anti-synergy cases. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1665](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1665.md)) from the Digital Library of the Commons copy (handle 10535/4512), printed pp. 178–208 of what appears to be the 1997 GAIA reprint, not the World Development pages; worth reading as the synthesis of the 1996 World Development special section on state-society synergy, and as the record's only access to Ostrom (1996), [LIT-2140](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2140.md), whose two cases and production functions it summarises. It holds that the useful support is a dependable public input the community cannot produce, given with continuing official contact, and that small-scale synergy can be built even in adverse settings, the limit being scaling up rather than prior social capital. A secondary synthesis of five articles plus Tendler, with no data of its own beyond an anecdote, positive cases chosen, and no measure of persistence after support ended; what it says of Ostrom is second-hand and in its own framing. |
| [LIT-2144](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2144.md) | An Aid-Institutions Paradox? A Review Essay on Aid Dependency and State Building in Sub-Saharan Africa | Moss, Pettersson & van de Walle (2006), CGD Working Paper 74. A review essay asking whether large aid sustained over decades weakens the recipient state's institutions, as resource rents do. It reviews four channels: macroeconomic and fiscal effects, including the soft budget constraint; donor practice, whose fragmentation and parallel structures draw staff and attention from the civil service; aid substituting for taxation, where the literature is negative on balance but "not a conclusive result", with grants and not loans associated with lower revenue; and accountability turned toward donors rather than citizens. Aid was meant as a temporary subsidy for revenue collection and institution building; in some three dozen countries it has stayed at a tenth of GNI or more for two decades. Following Kaldor, a state moves from aid dependency to self-sufficiency by learning to tax. They commit to no threshold, relaying Berg's 5 % and Clemens and Radelet's 15–45 % of GDP. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1661](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1661.md)) from the Center for Global Development's own PDF, the whole body (pp. 1–20) and the start of the references; worth reading as the review that joins the economists' tax-effort literature to the political science of revenue and state building, and as the clearest statement of how aid that was meant to be temporary became permanent in some three dozen African states. A review essay: its one original analysis is a bivariate figure whose thresholds it calls arbitrary, the econometrics it reviews are mixed, confounding and reverse causation are not excluded, and on exit from aid it has only the weaned cases of Korea, Taiwan and Botswana, without detail on how the taper was done. |
| [LIT-2148](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2148.md) | Sustaining Development: Results from a Study of Sustainability and Exit Strategies among Development Food Assistance Projects—India Country Study. Executive Summary | Rogers, Klemeyer, Bondre & Fierstein (2017). CARE and CRS ran Food for Peace projects in India from 1997 and gave their last cycle, a phase-out plan, to handing activities over to Government of India programmes; they exited in 2009 and 2010, and the endline survey was replicated two years later in a subset of states. Institutional deliveries in CRS areas, which "rose from 20 percent to 76 percent between baseline in 2002 and the end of the POP in 2010, continued to increase to 87 percent at follow-up in 2012", and irrigation through the employment guarantee grew; school meals lapsed where schools were late to join the Mid-Day Meals programme; stunting was not moved. Phase-over "depends critically on effective local implementation", and "the aggregate results for all states in the study mask substantial state-by-state differences". | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1655](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1655.md)) from the USAID DEC copy (PA00MNVN) on AidData's mirror of the DEC; worth reading as the study's test of phase-over, handing project activities to a state that already has resources, infrastructure and a legal duty to serve, and as the India half of the stand-in for the unread synthesis of the same study ([LIT-2151](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2151.md)). Health services and irrigation through the employment guarantee persisted or grew two years after exit, where the linkage ran before exit; school meals lapsed where the linkage was begun late; and differences between states were often larger than change over time. An executive summary of a two-year follow-up in a subset of states, with no comparison group, and assessing persistence of activities, not of impact, which on malnutrition was never shown. |
| [LIT-2149](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2149.md) | Why Do People Stay Poor? | Balboni, Bandiera, Burgess, Ghatak & Heil (2022; NBER 2021). BRAC's Targeting the Ultra-poor programme gave poor women in rural Bangladesh a one-off asset transfer, 91% of them choosing a cow, with roll-out randomized across 40 branch areas and about 6,000 households followed for 11 years. Among beneficiaries the four-year asset transition is S-shaped, with an unstable threshold of about 9,309 BDT (504 USD PPP), just above a cow's value. Those the transfer left below it "lose 14% of assets over the next four years while those who are pushed past the threshold grow their assets by 16%", and over 11 years those above gained land, self-employed hours, earnings and consumption. Control villages show no S. The authors test the poverty-trap view against differences "such as ability, talent or motivation" and conclude: "It is not their intrinsic characteristics that trap people in poverty but rather their circumstances." Threshold placement rests on non-random baseline assets, and the programme bundled consumption support, health support and training. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1654](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1654.md)) from NBER Working Paper 29340, the accepted text, on nber.org; the journal's copy at OUP was not reached (a Cloudflare check). Worth reading as the first long-run experimental test of a household asset poverty trap that locates the threshold: among ultra-poor women in rural Bangladesh given a one-off asset transfer, mostly a cow, those lifted above about 9,300 BDT gained assets, land, self-employed hours and consumption over 11 years, and those left just below lost assets. Its main limits: baseline assets, which place a household above or below the threshold, were not randomized (only the roll-out was); health and stress are not ruled out as mechanisms; the programme also gave consumption support, health support and training; crossing the threshold is no guarantee (fewer than half of young households above it kept the transfer's value); and in the NBER text the participation rates stated do not match Table I. |
| [LIT-2150](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2150.md) | Cash Transfers and Temptation Goods | Evans & Popova (2017; read as the 2014 World Bank working paper). A review of conditional and unconditional cash transfers in low- and middle-income countries, from a Google Scholar search narrowed to 19 studies with 44 estimates of impact on alcohol and tobacco, classified by sign and significance rather than pooled: 12 negative and significant, 24 negative and insignificant, 6 positive and insignificant, 2 positive and significant, both non-experimental and trivially small. Among 17 randomized estimates none is positive and significant. No difference between conditional and unconditional programs, by region or by duration of receipt. The authors conclude that "concerns that transfers will be used on alcohol and tobacco are unfounded". | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1649.md)) in its World Bank working-paper version, Policy Research Working Paper 6886 (May 2014), from the World Bank's own copy: body and Tables 1–10; the 2017 journal article was not read. Worth reading as the standard evidence against the stereotype that the poor spend unconditioned help on alcohol and tobacco: of 44 estimates from 19 studies, "82% of estimates are negative" and none of 17 randomized estimates is positive and significant. Its own limits: a count of estimates by sign and significance, not a meta-analysis, with no pooled effect, interval or publication-bias test, and with estimates within a study counted separately; all outcomes self-reported spending; only 8 of the 19 studies randomized; two internal inconsistencies between the text on p. 11 and Tables 5–6 (see the NOTE). No labour outcome. |

| [LIT-2154](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2154.md) | Sustaining Development: Results from a Study of Sustainability and Exit Strategies among Development Food Assistance Projects—Kenya Country Study. Executive Summary | Coates, Kegode, Galante & Blau (2016). Three Food for Peace projects in Kenya (ADRA, CARE, Food for the Hungry) ended in 2008–09 and were followed with three qualitative rounds and, in 2011, a replicated endline survey. "evidence of impact at the time of project exit did not necessarily predict sustainability 2–3 years later". Savings groups with no outside capital thrived; fee-for-service paravets and water committees largely held; volunteer health workers tied to an under-resourced Ministry of Health kept serving, but less; CARE's producer associations, weaned by graduated cost share, held where ADRA's, subsidised to the end, declined. It finds that impact at exit did not predict what lasted, and that the savings groups, paravets and water committees that held had their own resource stream, capacity, motivation and early linkages and had run on their own before exit, while activities fed by the project to the end declined. | [LIT-2156](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2156.md) | Aid Dependence Reconsidered | Azam, Devarajan & O'Connell (1999), World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 2144. A static public-finance problem, in which grant aid fills the gap between optimal spending and domestic revenue, gets Arrow-style learning by doing: the marginal cost of taxing is the reciprocal of accumulated revenue-collecting experience, which depreciates. A global planner who internalizes the learning faces two steady states, an efficient low-aid one that is a saddle and a high-aid, low-capacity one that is locally stable, and paths to the latter are fully rational. A planner who ignores institutions sets aid to the static gap: below a threshold of initial capacity aid rises until it finances the whole budget and tax capacity decays away; above it the economy converges to a low-aid state. Correction is an up-front cut in aid, which hurts the recipient in the short run; since the recipient prefers the high-aid state, graduation needs the gains passed back to it. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1682](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1682.md)) from the World Bank's own scan in its documents repository; worth reading as the short theory paper that gives "aid dependence" analytical content: learning by doing in tax collection, with grant aid filling the fiscal gap, yields a stable high-aid, low-capacity equilibrium beside an efficient saddle path, a threshold on initial institutions under gap-filling aid, and a donor–recipient conflict over graduation. Pure theory with strong functional forms (unit slopes, tax inefficiency the reciprocal of experience, fixed spending), one mechanism only, no test; the case readings are illustrative, and the printed formulas carry typos. A working paper whose cover asks that it not be cited without the authors' permission; no later published version was looked for. |
| [LIT-2158](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2158.md) | Place-Based Policies | Neumark & Simpson (2015; read as NBER w20049, 2014), a Handbook survey. Every result is the authors' summary of other studies. Theory (big push, multiple equilibria, agglomeration) could justify a temporary push that leaves an area self-sustaining, but evaluations mostly measure effects while incentives are in force. Enterprise-zone evidence is "very mixed": gains are often relocation from nearby areas, or capitalized into land and house values with higher-income residents arriving. Monitored, conditional grants raise employment and investment in recipients but not productivity, and in one Italian study investment fell below controls after the last payment. Infrastructure and public goods look best: the Tennessee Valley Authority's manufacturing gains outlasted its transfers through agglomeration while its direct effect and its farm gains did not, and the agglomeration gain is estimated to net to about zero nationally. Verdict: no place-based policy has been shown to create self-sustaining gains. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1656](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1656.md)) from NBER Working Paper 20049 (April 2014, revised August 2014) on NBER's own site, a pre-publication draft; the Handbook chapter itself, paywalled at Elsevier, was not read. Worth reading as a map of the US and European evidence on place-based policy (enterprise and empowerment zones, discretionary grants, clusters and universities, the Tennessee Valley Authority, the Appalachian Regional Commission and EU Structural Funds, community development), and for its verdict that even the best of it "does not establish that they create self-sustaining economic gains". Every result in it is the authors' summary of other studies, none read here; most evaluations cover the years while incentives were in force, so the evidence on what outlasts support rests on effectively one study, of the TVA. US and Europe only. |
| [LIT-2160](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2160.md) | A multifaceted program causes lasting progress for the very poor: Evidence from six countries | Banerjee, Duflo, Goldberg, Karlan, Osei, Parienté, Shapiro, Thuysbaert & Udry (2015). Six randomized trials of BRAC's Graduation program, in Ethiopia, Ghana, Honduras, India, Pakistan and Peru, with 10,495 of the poorest households: a one-time productive asset, consumption support for 4 to 13 months, training, frequent coaching visits, savings and health services, for about two years. One year after all support ended, 8 of 10 pooled indices were still significant, with "no evidence of mean reversion" in consumption, food security or assets; income and working time fell back somewhat but stayed positive; adults worked 17.5 more minutes a day at the end of the program and 11.2 more a year later. Benefits exceeded costs at five sites, Honduras, where the chickens died, being the exception. The authors say the durability supports a poverty trap, but that modest average effects also fit a "poverty flat", with persistence and no take-off. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1669](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1669.md)) from the publisher's typeset PDF posted by the MIT Economics department, the institution of the first two authors; worth reading as the multi-site test of whether a time-limited "big push" to the poorest households leaves them working and earning more after the support stops, and as direct evidence against reading support to the poor as producing slack effort: adults worked more, not less, during the program and one year after it. Six RCTs, 10,495 households; most gains held one year after all support ended. Its own limits: a bundle, so no component is identified; follow-up only one year past the end; large differences between sites (Honduras faded, Peru weak); 52% take-up in India; self-reported outcomes; the supplementary tables S1–S6 were not read. The authors read the durability as support for a poverty trap, then argue against their own reading. |
| [LIT-2161](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2161.md) | Slum Clearance and Urban Renewal in the United States | Collins & Shester (2013; NBER 2011, revised 2012). A city-level instrumental-variable study of federal urban renewal grants under Title I of the Housing Act of 1949 in 458 US cities, the instrument being the years a city could take part, set by when its state passed enabling legislation. Each year of eligibility brought about $10 of grants per capita (first-stage F 13.8), and rural counties show no relationship between the legislation and outcomes. In 1980 "a $100 per capita difference in grant funding is associated with a 2.4 percent difference in 1980 median income and a 6.9 percent difference in 1980 median property value", with 9–11% more population and housing units; the effects "are not driven by changes in demographic composition", appear for income by 1960 and property value by 1970, and in 2000 "do not dissipate with time". The authors read this as raised local productivity, and say the design cannot price the costs borne by the more than 300,000 families the projects displaced. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1683](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1683.md)) from NBER Working Paper 17458, the November 2012 revision, on nber.org; the published AEJ text was not read. Worth reading as the first well-identified estimate of what federal urban renewal under Title I of the Housing Act of 1949 did to whole cities: instrumenting grants with the years a state's enabling legislation let a city take part, $100 more per 1950 resident went with about 2.4% higher median family income, 6.9% higher median property value and 9–11% more population and housing units in 1980, effects not explained by a changed racial or educational composition and not faded by 2000, decades after new funding ended in 1974. Its main limits: the data are city aggregates, so the 300,000-odd families displaced, the neighbourhoods cleared and any social organization are outside the design; the instrument's variation lies mostly outside the Northeast and Midwest; county effects are weak, so gains may be relocation within metropolitan areas; and the 2000 estimates are imprecise. |
| [LIT-2164](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2164.md) | Looking Like a State: Techniques of Persistent Failure in State Capability for Implementation | Pritchett, Woolcock & Andrews (2012 working paper; Journal of Development Studies 2013). Governance indicators show many states with low capability that is barely rising: at their implied pace since independence the bottom 15 would take 672 years on average to reach Singapore's level, and on ICRG data since 1985 the median rate of change is zero and most of the bottom 30 are falling. The paper asks how states and donors keep up the business of reform without acquiring capability, and names two techniques: isomorphic mimicry, keeping legitimacy by imitating the forms of functional organizations, and premature load bearing, loading fledgling organizations with tasks too complex too soon. A framework of agents, organizations and systems places the cause in whether a system requires, recognizes and rewards novelty. Cash on Delivery aid is offered, unevaluated, as a way to reward function. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1678](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1678.md)) from the CID Working Paper 239 copy on the Harvard Kennedy School site; worth reading for the estimate that makes the capability trap a matter of centuries (bottom-15 countries 672 years to Singapore's measured capability at their pace since independence; a median ICRG rate of change of zero since 1985) and for naming two techniques of persistent failure, isomorphic mimicry and premature load bearing. The estimates are linear extrapolations of perception-based, rescaled indicators; premature load bearing is named and defined but hardly developed in this version; the journal version was not seen. |

Prizes randomly assigned within cells of three Swedish lotteries (prize-linked savings accounts, the Kombi subscription lottery and the Triss scratch-card lottery, paid as a lump sum or in monthly instalments), won by players aged 21–64 and matched to tax and wage registers for 1991–2010. Winning cuts gross labour earnings by about 1.1 SEK a year per 100 SEK won, "immediately" and for more than ten years, about 0.58 SEK after tax; mostly through hours (1.3 hours a week per 1M SEK), less through leaving work; self-employment falls too. The effect barely varies by age, sex, education, lottery, form of payment or prize size. A calibrated life-cycle model puts the average lifetime marginal propensity to earn at −0.11, larger for younger winners. Spouses cut their earnings by less than winners, against income pooling. The authors call the response "modest". | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1648](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1648.md)) in the authors' NBER Working Paper 21762 of November 2015, not in the AER version of 2017, whose text and Online Appendix were not read; worth reading as the cleanest evidence held on what a large, unconditional and permanent windfall does to work: prizes randomly assigned within cells of three Swedish lotteries, matched to tax and wage registers for up to twenty years, cut winners' gross labour earnings by about 1.1 SEK a year per 100 SEK won, at once and for more than ten years, mostly through fewer hours, with little difference by age, sex, education or prize size; spouses cut theirs by less than half as much. The authors call the response modest. | [LIT-2168](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2168.md) | Planning Ahead for Better Neighborhoods: Long-Run Evidence from Tanzania | Michaels, Nigmatulina, Rauch, Regan, Baruah & Dahlstrand (2021). A spatial regression discontinuity against adjacent land also unbuilt at the start finds that by the 2010s de novo areas have larger, more regularly laid out and better-connected buildings, higher hedonic values and roads and mains that are still there; a third of the quality gap is owner sorting. Upgrading areas are, descriptively, no better than comparison areas and their infrastructure deteriorated. A model explains the contrast by a threshold: infrastructure stays high-quality only if enough owners can invest, and existing low-quality housing is not rebuilt until it is destroyed. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1651](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1651.md)) from the authors' accepted manuscript of 14 November 2020 in LSE Research Online; worth reading as a rare long-run test of one-off public support that residents built on: greenfield plots, roads and water mains laid out in 1975–84 carried, by the 2010s, larger and better housing and roads and mains that were still there, while the same spending in already-built squatter areas left no gain and decayed, which the authors explain by a feedback between owners' investment and the upkeep of infrastructure. | [LIT-2170](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2170.md) | Long-Term Effects of the Targeting the Ultra Poor Program | Banerjee, Duflo & Sharma (2021; NBER working paper 2020). A ten-year randomized follow-up of the Targeting the Ultra Poor program run by Bandhan in West Bengal from 2007: a productive asset (mostly livestock), 30–40 weeks of consumption support, savings and weekly visits for 18 months, after which "Bandhan had no contact with beneficiary households". Effects on consumption (0.6 SD at year 10), food security, income (0.3 SD) and health "grow for the first seven years following the transfer and persist until year 10"; treated adults work more at every wave. The control group also grew fast, from $1.35 to $2.9 a day, and the treated pulled ahead by taking better advantage of wage work and migration; the authors read a big push as complementary to macroeconomic growth. They call the pattern consistent with escape from a poverty trap, and equally with persistent effects without one. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1667](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1667.md)) as NBER Working Paper 28074 (November 2020, revised June 2021), not the AER: Insights version of record; worth reading as the longest randomized follow-up on the record of a one-time push to the poorest households: in West Bengal the effects on consumption, income and health grew for seven years and held to year ten, although the implementer had no contact with households after 18 months, and treated adults worked more at every wave. Its own limits: one site, the most favourable of the six in Banerjee et al. (2015); 978 households, of whom 266 of 514 offered took part, so ITT; 71% tracked across all four waves; the control group's own fast growth; the authors hold the pattern consistent with, not proof of, escape from a poverty trap. | [LIT-2174](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2174.md) v2 | Aid, Incentives, and Sustainability: An Institutional Analysis of Development Cooperation | Ostrom, Gibson, Shivakumar & Andersson (2002), a study commissioned by Sida's evaluation department. They frame development as solving collective-action problems, with "missing institutions" rather than missing money as the deficit, and catalogue the incentive problems aid itself creates across an eight-actor system that "lacks important error-correcting mechanisms": the Samaritan's dilemma, moral hazard and soft budget constraints, fungibility and crowding-out, bought conditionality, principal–agent chains, disbursement pressure inside the donor and evaluations nobody demands. In the type case, infrastructure whose upkeep the donor predictably supplies is not maintained by the recipient and is rebuilt from outside (Kafue Gorge, Zambia). Benefits outlast the aid only with beneficiary ownership: stating the demand, contributing some of their own assets, getting the benefits and sharing in the decision to continue or stop, "a necessary, though not sufficient, condition". A later version is the Oxford University Press book The Samaritan's Dilemma (Gibson, Andersson, Ostrom & Shivakumar, 2005), not registered here. | Active — read 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1647](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1647.md), Read on the parts its argument uses) from Sida's own PDF on its publications CDN; worth reading as the record's first work on foreign aid, and as the Ostrom school's account of how predictable outside help lowers a recipient's own upkeep (the Samaritan's dilemma) and of the four conditions of beneficiary ownership under which benefits outlast the aid. Its evidence is theory, a literature review, 175-odd interviews (63 structured, with Sida staff) and five short illustrative field cases in Zambia and India, about ten person-days a site; no counterfactual, and sustainability is forecast from incentives, not observed after exit. One donor, Sida, around 2000. |

| [LIT-2178](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2178.md) | Gift-giving and reciprocity in global society: Introducing Marcel Mauss in international studies | Heins, Unrau & Avram (2018). The introduction to a special issue on Mauss in international relations. A gift is "the generous transfer of socially valued objects without any (legal or contractual) guarantee of reciprocation" that yet obliges a return; unreturned, it "poisons" relationships (p. 127). Mauss's potlatch is agonistic and builds hierarchy, his kula circular and builds a lasting connection (p. 128). The aid case is Dillon (1968) on the Marshall Plan: the French could not repay and responded with resentment, and Dillon proposed a kula-like circular reciprocity as the better model for gifts between nations (pp. 131–132). The rest places Mauss as a solidarist rationalist in Wight's scheme and introduces the issue's papers. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1679](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1679.md)) from the published version in DuEPublico, the University of Duisburg-Essen's repository; worth reading as a short, quotable introduction to Mauss's gift for international relations: the obligations to give, receive and reciprocate, the unreturned gift that "poisons" relationships, the agonistic potlatch against the circular kula, and Dillon's account of the Marshall Plan in France as a gift the French could not repay and met with resentment. An introduction to a special issue and a map of the literature: its aid evidence is one secondary study, Dillon (1968), and it says nothing of development aid since, of grants and loans, or of dependence and exit. Read also as the stand-in for Hattori (2001), [LIT-2180](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2180.md), but only for the attribution that Hattori draws on Mauss, not for his argument. |
