| [LIT-2182](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2182.md) | Revenues, State Formation, and the Quality of Governance in Developing Countries | Moore (2004). A review essay naming the fiscal (social) contract proposition: states that depend on broadly levied taxes tend toward accountable, representative government, because earned income obliges the state to build a bureaucracy, stay present on the ground and bargain with taxpayers. Rentier states live off unearned income, natural-resource rents and strategic rents, whose dominant modern form is development aid, and those capacities are not built or are let decay. The oil evidence is others' cross-national work, which he accepts; the aid evidence he calls weak and possibly reverse-caused. He declines to say whether more reliance on taxation would pay a governance dividend, and lists instead the conditions under which states negotiate with taxpayers rather than coerce them; easy concessional finance pulls governments away from negotiating. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1663](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1663.md)) from the journal's typeset version of record as deposited in the UK Department for International Development's research-outputs store; worth reading as the compact statement of the fiscal-contract proposition and of aid as a rent, the political-science side of the question how an aid-dependent state comes to support itself. A review and agenda essay with no data of its own: the oil evidence it accepts is others' cross-national work, the aid evidence it calls confounded and possibly reverse-caused, and it says nothing measured about tapering or withdrawal of aid, declining to answer whether more reliance on taxation would bring a governance dividend. |

The Financial Consequences of Winning the Lottery | Hankins, Hoekstra & Skiba (2011). 34,987 first-time Florida Fantasy 5 winners of $600 to $150,000, 1993–2002, linked by name and county to every Florida bankruptcy filing. Conditional on winning, the amount is as good as random. Winners of $50,000–150,000 were about half as likely as winners of under $10,000 to file in the two years after winning (−1.63 points) and more likely to file three to five years after (+1.21 points), so that within five years no difference was detected (−0.42 points, se 0.78). Large winners who filed had net assets and unsecured debt like small winners who filed, though the median large prize, $65,000 before tax, exceeded the $52,000 of unsecured debt of the most distressed players. The authors conclude the money postpones rather than prevents bankruptcy. Read from the 2009 working draft; the numbers are the draft's. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1673](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1673.md)), tables included and figures not, from the authors' working draft of 2009-02-16 posted on UC Berkeley's Labor Lunch seminar page; the published REStat article was not read (SSRN and the Vanderbilt repository showed Cloudflare checks). Worth reading as the first causal estimate of whether a large unconditional lump sum prevents bankruptcy: among Florida Fantasy 5 winners, those who won $50,000–150,000 were half as likely as winners of under $10,000 to file in the two years after winning and more likely to file in years 3–5, with no detectable difference over five years, and the large winners who filed had similar net assets and unsecured debt. Its main limits: the numbers are the draft's; the $50,000–150,000 band holds 1,212 winners and 12 filings within two years; the year 3–5 rise is marginal and not significant in the probit or the one-play-per-card subsample; the five-year result is no detectable effect, with a wide interval, not a proven zero; the balance-sheet comparison rests on 47 against 103 filers; bankruptcy is the only outcome; and the mechanisms are listed, not tested. |
| [LIT-2186](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2186.md) | Debunking the Stereotype of the Lazy Welfare Recipient: Evidence from Cash Transfer Programs | Banerjee, Hanna, Kreindler & Olken (2017). The household micro-data of seven cluster-randomized evaluations of government-run, non-contributory cash transfer programmes (Honduras PRAF II, Morocco Tayssir, Mexico Progresa and PAL, Philippines Pantawid, Indonesia PKH, Nicaragua RPS) are re-analysed on harmonized definitions of work for adults aged 16–65 and pooled with a Bayesian hierarchical model. No programme changes weekly hours; only one, Honduras, changes participation (−3 points, at the 10% level). Pooled and scaled to a transfer worth 13.6% of consumption, participation moves −0.4 points (90% interval −2.3 to +1.4) and hours −0.08 a week (−1.7 to +1.4), "broadly symmetric around zero"; men's moderate reductions are ruled out, women's interval is wide. Its main limits: support was still being paid throughout (one to two years in), so it says nothing about dependence after withdrawal; transfers were small (4–20% of consumption) and weakly means-tested; no African or South Asian trial qualified; the pooled intervals are 90% credible intervals; the online appendices, where attrition and balance would be, were not read. |
| [LIT-2187](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2187.md) | Escaping Capability Traps Through Problem Driven Iterative Adaptation (PDIA) | Andrews, Pritchett & Woolcock (2012 working paper; World Development 2013). Development interventions reward recipient governments for adopting the forms of capable states (best-practice laws, agencies and procedures, scored by indicators such as PEFA, the World Governance Indicators and Doing Business) rather than demonstrated function, and the reward is a continuing flow of external money and legitimacy. The result is isomorphic mimicry and a "capability trap" in which capability stagnates or declines while reform rhetoric and aid continue. The proposed escape, PDIA, builds capability through locally nominated problems, authorized experimentation, tight feedback and broad engagement. Donor projects succeed at "logistical" tasks and fail at implementation-intensive capability building. Argued from examples; no new data and no evaluation of PDIA. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1664](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1664.md)) from the Harvard Kennedy School working-paper copy (HKS RWP12-036, which contains CGD Working Paper 299); worth reading as the source of "isomorphic mimicry" and the "capability trap" in development practice, and of PDIA, the four-principle account of how an aid-dependent state organization builds capability of its own: locally nominated problems, an authorizing environment for positive deviance, tight feedback loops and broad engagement. A conceptual essay with no new data: its examples are anecdotal or hypothetical, PDIA is not evaluated, and it is silent on own revenue, aid volume and what happens when aid is withdrawn. The journal version was not seen. |
| [LIT-2188](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2188.md) | Blazing Grace: The Gifted Culture of Burning Man | St John (2017), NANO 11. A cultural anthropologist reads Burning Man as a "gift culture" through Lewis Hyde's The Gift. Its Gifting principle, which he quotes, says a gift's value is unconditional and that gifting "does not contemplate a return". The recipient has no obligation to reciprocate, yet such gifts "inspire gratitude and thus a response that keeps the gift in motion" (p. 5): Sahlins's generalized reciprocity, beside the balanced reciprocity of swapped trinkets. The return goes not to the giver but to the community, in later labour, as recipients come to identify with the gift, that is, with Burning Man. He sets this against Mauss's gift, whose obligation can turn against the one who fails to honour it, while granting that such relations can be seen at Burning Man too. The most pressing threat is non-participation: spectators, paying tourists and the "Plug-n-Play" camps exposed in 2014, answered in part by reforming theme-camp registration and placement. He ends with the Burning Man Project's 2016 turn to patronage, or "matronage", to fund artists. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1662](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1662.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF; registered as the stand-in for Harvey (2004), [LIT-2175](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2175.md), whose page was not reached. Worth reading as a first-hand ethnographer's account of how Burning Man's gift culture is meant to work: gifts that oblige no return to the giver yet circulate through gratitude returned to the community, read through Hyde's The Gift against Mauss's gift that obliges, and how the 2014 "Sherpagate" crisis of paid, non-participating camps was met. It quotes the Gifting principle verbatim and lists the ten, but quotes no other principle. An interpretive essay in a humanities journal, built largely on the organization's own Philosophical Center writings, with no data on how often gifts are returned or how many participants free-ride. |
| [LIT-2189](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2189.md) | The effects of cash transfers on adult labor market outcomes | Baird, McKenzie & Özler (2018), a structured narrative review, "not ... a formal systematic literature review/meta-analysis", of experimental and quasi-experimental studies of adult work and earnings under government conditional and unconditional transfers, pensions, charitable and humanitarian cash, remittances, job-search subsidies, business grants and graduation programs in low- and middle-income countries. Worth reading as the standard overview of how adults' work and earnings respond to cash transfers in low- and middle-income countries, and as a direct test of the stereotype that assured help makes the poor work less: prime-age adults' work barely changes, pensioners work less, and transfers for job search or business start-up raise work. A field review of condominial sewerage, block-level feeder lines with layouts residents choose and reduced tariffs, built over twelve years in seven Brazilian cities. In roughly half the cases it "performed as well as conventional sewerage, but cost between a third to a quarter of those systems"; others suffered low connection rates, poor construction and neglect, problems the author calls institutional. The design devolves feeder upkeep to residents, which "has not worked well even in the best cases": block cooperation rarely formed, and the agencies' retreat "created a void of service provision". Service lasted where agencies stayed in face-to-face contact and organised residents held them to account. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 (NOTE-1659) from the World Bank's Documents & Reports PDF, a scan with poor OCR, Annex II's comic-strip manual apart; worth reading as the primary field account of Brazilian condominial sewerage, the case Ostrom (1996), [LIT-2140](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2140.md), uses per Evans, and as direct evidence on what happens when an agency steps back from a coproduced service. | [LIT-2191](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2191.md) | Essai sur le don. Forme et raison de l'échange dans les sociétés archaïques | Mauss (1925). A comparative essay on exchange in Polynesia, Melanesia, the American Northwest coast and ancient laws, asking what force in a thing given makes its recipient return it. Exchange there takes the form of gifts voluntary in theory and obligatory in fact, between collectivities, under three obligations: to give, to receive and to return. In Maori law the thing carries the giver's hau, which seeks its origin through every holder; in the potlatch the return is due with interest, and failing it costs face, rank and in the limit freedom (debt slavery). The conclusion holds that the same morality survives: an unreturned gift still makes its acceptor inferior and charity wounds, social insurance is right as a return owed to the worker for labour given, and the individual must still be made to rely on himself. | Active — skimmed 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1658](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1658.md); introduction, chapter I, part of chapter II and the conclusion read in full) from the Classiques des sciences sociales digital edition, transcribed from PUF's Sociologie et anthropologie (1968); worth reading as the founding statement of the three obligations of the gift (to give, to receive, to return) and for its claim that a gift accepted without return subordinates the receiver, which Mauss carries into a defence of social insurance as a return owed to the worker. Comparative and interpretive, built on second-hand ethnography; the hau reading rests on one informant's text in a translation Mauss himself calls abridged; the conclusion is moral and political argument, not a finding. |

| [LIT-2201](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2201.md) v2 | A search for multiple equilibria in urban industrial structure | Davis & Weinstein (2004 working paper; J. Regional Science 2008). A threshold-regression test that puts unique and multiple equilibria on an even footing: under a unique equilibrium, shock and recovery growth lie on one line of slope −1 through the origin; under multiple equilibria on parallel lines with ordered intercepts beyond thresholds. Applied to the Allied bombing of Japan for city population, aggregate manufacturing in up to 114 cities, and eight manufacturing industries: "The data provide no support for the existence of multiple equilibria." Cities recover their population, their manufacturing share and even their specific industries; industry recovery is slower where hit hardest (ρ about 0.34, indistinguishable from zero without Hiroshima). | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1690](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1690.md), Read: sections I–V, Tables 1–7, the references and the data appendix) from NBER Working Paper 10252 (January 2004) on NBER's own site, not from the Journal of Regional Science version of record; worth reading as the direct test, by threshold regression, of whether the Allied bombing of Japan moved cities to different equilibria, putting unique and multiple equilibria on an even footing, and as the extension from city population to city manufacturing and eight industries. It finds a unique stable equilibrium at every level; slower recovery where industries were hit hardest is the authors' possible reason, not a finding. Its limits: thresholds are assumed common across cities in log units and each city's dynamics independent of the others'; the test examines necessary conditions within that structure; industry-level power is limited; and the authors themselves set apart greenfield investment as a different question. |
| [LIT-2205](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2205.md) | Bones, Bombs, and Break Points: The Geography of Economic Activity | Davis & Weinstein (2002). Sets increasing returns, random growth and locational fundamentals against 8,000 years of Japanese regional density and against the Allied bombing of 303 Japanese cities. Instrumenting 1940–47 population growth with deaths and buildings destroyed per capita, 1947–60 growth undoes it one for one (coefficient −1.048), about three-quarters once 1925–40 trend growth is controlled (−0.759), and wholly by 1965 (−1.027); Hiroshima and Nagasaki return to their prewar trends. Reconstruction subsidies mattered little. The authors reject random growth and find that spatial catastrophes from temporary shocks are "not a central tendency borne out in the data", favouring locational fundamentals. | [LIT-2219](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2219.md) | Aid Dependence and the Quality of Governance: Cross-Country Empirical Tests | Knack (2000 working paper; 2001 journal version not read). Across 80 aid-receiving countries, the change in the ICRG quality-of-governance index from 1982 (or 1984) to 1995 is regressed on mean aid relative to GNP or to government spending, with initial governance, population change and income growth controlled. Higher aid goes with less improvement (OLS −0.067 per point of aid/GNP); instrumented with recipient need and donor interest the effect roughly doubles (−0.154). It holds for aid/GNP in the 31 African countries, is several times larger for technical assistance, does not vary with initial governance, and shrinks as aid becomes more variable. The mechanisms, among them the tax bargain, are argued and not tested. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1707](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1707.md)) in its working-paper version, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 2396 of July 2000, from the World Bank's own public-disclosure scan; the 2001 journal text was not read and its estimates may differ. Worth reading as an early instrumented cross-country test of the thesis that aid dependence erodes institutions, and for its moderators: across 80 countries, 1982–95, higher mean aid goes with smaller gains in the ICRG governance index, the effect roughly doubles under two-stage least squares, holds for aid/GNP within Africa, is several times larger for technical assistance, does not depend on initial governance, and weakens as aid becomes less predictable. One change score per country, instruments whose exclusion is only tested by overidentification, no first stage reported, no tax or revenue variable, and a standard error that differs between two tables for the same specification. |

Read on 2026-11-12 in [NOTE-1779](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1779.md): FairCert is a black-box audit pipeline that turns per-group false-positive-rate (FPR) and true-positive-rate (TPR) gaps into finite-sample certificates. Five stages: a stratified split with a walled-off 15% audit set; LLM-guided discovery of candidate intersectional subgroups from aggregate training statistics (hypotheses), confirmed on the disjoint audit set; per-group error rates of the classifier's predictions; a certificate built from Clopper-Pearson exact intervals per group with a Bonferroni correction over K groups, which bounds the worst pairwise gap with probability at least 1−δ and passes if the bound is within tolerance ε; and, for failures, per-group threshold calibration with the TPR cost reported, plus a structured EU AI Act-oriented report. Its account is [THEORY-1660](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1660.md). Registered from the exchange "Medical Ethics and Media Enshitification" (2026-11-11), where A cited it at A42 §6. | Active |

| [LIT-2473](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2473.md) | Configuring E-Government Services Using Ontologies | Dimitris Apostolou, Ljiljana Stojanović, Tomás Pariente Lobo, Jofre Casas Miró and Andreas Papadakis (2005), e-Commerce, e-Business, e-Government (I3E 2005), IFIP, pp. 141–155, DOI 10.1007/0-387-29773-1_10. The paper presents OntoGov (IST-2002-507237), an ontology platform for configuring and reconfiguring e-government services consistently when law or organization changes. | [LIT-2482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2482.md) v2 | An Institutional Framework for Policy Analysis and Design | Polski and Ostrom (2017), An Institutional Framework For Policy Analysis. The chapter presents the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework as a tool for policy analysts. The analysis proceeds in steps: - Define the policy problem and the analysis's objectives. - Analyse the physical and material conditions, the community attributes and the rules-in-use. - Integrate the analysis around the action arena: the action situation and its actors. - Evaluate patterns of interaction and outcomes. **Institutions** are "widely understood" rules, norms or strategies. **Rules-in-use** come in seven types, each matched to an element of the action situation: 1. position 2. boundary 3. authority 4. aggregation 5. scope 6. information 7. payoff **Levels of rules.** For policy systems, rules are nested at three levels: - operating (or operational) rules govern day-to-day choices; - collective-choice rules govern who may change operating rules, and how; - constitutional rules govern who may craft collective-choice rules, and how. The worked example is US interstate bank branching before and after 1994. Read for the exchange "luria experiment design". | Active — Skimmed on 2026-11-12 ([NOTE-1842](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1842.md)) from https://ostromworkshop.indiana.edu/doc/teaching/iad-for-policy-applications.pdf. |
| [LIT-2486](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2486.md) | A Systematic Approach to Institutional Analysis: Applying Crawford and Ostrom's Grammar | Xavier Basurto, Gordon Kingsley, Kelly McQueen, Mshadoni Smith and Christopher M. Weible (2010), Political Research Quarterly 63(3):523–537, DOI 10.1177/1065912909334430. The first empirical application of Crawford and Ostrom's grammatical syntax: two pieces of US legislation (the metropolitan planning organization section of TEA-21, and a Georgia abortion bill) are partitioned into institutional statements, coded by the five components, classified as strategies, norms or rules, and analysed in nested form around a focal attribute. Intercoder reliability is reported and the hardest coding decisions are listed as open problems for the syntax. Registered on 2026-11-12 as a stand-in for [LIT-2309](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2309.md); it applies and restates the grammar's components and coding rules, not Crawford and Ostrom's argument for them. | Active — Read on 2026-11-12. (2021), OBO Foundry in 2021: operationalizing open data principles to evaluate ontologies. The OBO Foundry's operations committee reports how it turned the Foundry's founding principles (open, common format, URI space, versioning, scope, textual definitions, relations, documentation, plurality of users, collaboration, locus of authority, naming, maintenance, responsiveness) into operational rules stated in MUST/SHOULD language, each with an automated check, run across all member ontologies and shown on a public dashboard. It first re-curated the registry metadata of every ontology (moving it into a GitHub repository changed by pull request), then refined each principle into a checkable procedure, then built the dashboard on ROBOT. Errors fell after the dashboard was announced; some principles cannot be automated. Read in full ([NOTE-1941](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1941.md)). Artifacts embody power in two ways: a design or arrangement settles an issue in a community (Moses's low parkway overpasses; the tomato harvester), and "inherently political technologies" require, or are strongly compatible with, particular political relations (the bomb; nuclear power). "By far the greatest latitude of choice exists the very first time" a technique is introduced, and "the original flexibility vanishes for all practical purposes once the initial commitments are made". Collision Between Vehicle Controlled by Developmental Automated Driving System and Pedestrian, Tempe, Arizona, March 18, 2018. NTSB/HAR-19/03 (PB2019-101402). The NTSB found the probable cause to be the operator's failure to monitor the road and the automated system, through distraction by her phone. Uber ATG's inadequate risk assessment, operator oversight and countermeasures to automation complacency, "all a consequence of its inadequate safety culture", contributed, as did the impaired pedestrian's crossing and Arizona's oversight. The system was designed to rely on the operator to avoid collisions, and ATG's culture contributed to the operator's distraction itself. The report disclaims fault and blame. Read 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2034](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2034.md), [THEORY-1932](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1932.md)). | [LIT-2665](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2665.md) v3 | Moral Crumple Zones: Cautionary Tales in Human-Robot Interaction | Elish (2019). Moral Crumple Zones: Cautionary Tales in Human-Robot Interaction. Engaging Science, Technology, and Society 5: 40-60. DOI 10.17351/ests2019.260. Elish names the moral crumple zone: when control over an automated system is distributed, responsibility for its failure can be misattributed to the nearest human operator, who had limited control, so that the operator absorbs moral and legal blame and "the integrity of the technological system" is protected. She argues it from the reception of Three Mile Island and Air France 447, through media framing, certification and the operator's legal final authority, and expects it of self-driving cars. Read 2026-11-16 ([NOTE-2019](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2019.md), [THEORY-1928](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1928.md)). Owning Decisions: AI Decision-Support and the Attributability-Gap. Science and Engineering Ethics 30(4): 27. DOI 10.1007/s11948-024-00485-1. Argues, with Watson's and Shoemaker's accountability, attributability and answerability, that AI decision support threatens responsibility chiefly as attributability: a decision made with a tool that presupposes outcome-shaping values the user has not endorsed is hers in name but does not express her value-judgements. The gap comes in degrees and descriptive tools open it too; remedies are endorsement through transparency, value calibration and confining tools to description. Read; the reading is [NOTE-2007](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2007.md) and [THEORY-1915](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1915.md). Governance in the Banking Sector. November 2026 (file of 2 November). A non- binding discussion paper. The HKMA proposes "intent-anchored accountability": an AI agent in a bank should act only for an approved business intent, within delegated authority that is defined in advance, technically enforced through an "agent harness" (least-privilege permissions, deterministic checks, transaction and velocity limits, approval gates) and changed only through change control, with a named accountable owner. Where oversight cannot keep pace, the agent's authority, scope or velocity should be cut. | [LIT-2707](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2707.md) | "Making Out" While Driving: Relational and Efficiency Games in the Gig Economy | Cameron (2022), Organization Science 33(1): 231-252. Four years of fieldwork with ride-hail drivers (participant observation, 136 interviews with 63 drivers) find that, without managers or coworkers, drivers make their work meaningful through two workplace games: a relational game scored by the app's customer ratings, in which the platform appears as a facilitator and drivers follow its suggestions, and an efficiency game tracked with their own tools and sometimes by manipulating the algorithm, in which it appears as an opponent. Both produce engagement; the paper does not claim they produce consent. Read 2026-11-16 as a partial stand-in for Cameron (2024), [LIT-2686](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2686.md): same fieldwork, the precursor of its two tactics, not its concepts of constant and confined choices or choice-based consent. It bears on [QUESTION-461](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-461.md). | Active — Read 2026-11-16 in the author's post-review manuscript (Oct 2021) on the Wharton faculty site, as a partial stand-in for Cameron (2024), [LIT-2686](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2686.md), which is Unfetched. |

In a simulated hiring screen on census data, four upstream choices (label definition, feature measurement, model-selection metric, validation strategy) are varied; three move the counterfactual explanations given to rejected candidates more than the explanation method's own validity threshold does. Accountability, narrowly, is "a relationship between an actor and a forum, in which the actor has an obligation to explain and to justify his or her conduct, the forum can pose questions and pass judgement, and the actor may face consequences"; whether a practice is accountability is an either/or question, kept apart from typing it on four dimensions and assessing it from three perspectives. Answerability is its interrogation stage; forums are often not principals, and "the consequences are not necessarily brought upon the actor by the forum itself". It corroborates [CLAIM-739](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-739.md) and qualifies [TERM-126](../../../record/terms.d/TERM-126.md); [QUESTION-480](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-480.md) is left open ([THEORY-1976](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1976.md)). | Active — read in full 2026-11-17 ([NOTE-2069](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2069.md)) from the publisher's version in Utrecht University's open repository; worth reading as the standard statement of the actor–forum account of accountability, which corroborates [CLAIM-739](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-739.md) and places answerability inside accountability, the reverse of [TERM-126](../../../record/terms.d/TERM-126.md)'s nesting. |

| [LIT-2740](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2740.md) v2 | A Ladder Of Citizen Participation | Sherry R. Arnstein (1969), Journal of the American Institute of Planners 35(4): 216–224. Citizen participation is citizen power, the redistribution of power to the have-nots. Her eight-rung ladder runs from non-participation (manipulation, therapy) through tokenism (informing, consultation, placation), where citizens may hear and be heard but lack the power to ensure they are heeded, to citizen power (partnership, delegated power, citizen control), illustrated from 1960s federal programs. Administrative burden is a function of the learning, psychological and compliance costs citizens bear in dealing with the state; its level and its distribution between state and individual are often a deliberate political choice, and its opacity suits hidden politics. | [LIT-2771](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2771.md) | Toward a Standard Approach to Operationalizing Coercive Control and Classifying Violence Types | Hardesty, Crossman, Haselschwerdt, Raffaelli, Ogolsky and Johnson (2015). In 190 divorcing mothers, scoring coercive control by how often tactics are used, rather than how many, gives stable high- and low-control groups (a PMWI Dominance–Isolation cutoff of 19). Crossed with any violence, this yields no violence/low control, situational couple violence, nonviolent coercive control and coercive controlling violence; the two violent groups differ in fear, threat and harassment even with the frequency and severity of violence held constant, so the differences "reflect the control context rather than differences in violence". Registered as the read neighbour of Johnson 2008, [LIT-2715](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2715.md). It corroborates [CLAIM-709](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-709.md). | Active — read in full 2026-11-17 ([NOTE-2046](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2046.md)) from the author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC4553695), as a read neighbour of Johnson (2008), [LIT-2715](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2715.md), which could not be read; Johnson is its last author. Worth reading here for an operational test of the typology's two main types and for its finding that the group differences track the control context with the amount of violence held constant. |
| [LIT-2772](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2772.md) | Coercive Control (testimony on H.103 to the Vermont House Committee on Judiciary) | Evan Stark (2015), written testimony to the Vermont House Committee on Judiciary on H.103. Coercive control is "a strategic course of oppressive behavior" combining violence, intimidation, isolation and control "to dominate, exploit and/or subjugate a partner and deprive them of basic rights and liberties". Its violence is typically frequent and low-level; many of its tactics, "taken alone, may not rise to the level of abuse" but make the pattern in combination; it violates "autonomy, dignity and liberty" as well as safety; and "Interventions focused on discrete assaults" miss it. Registered as the read neighbour of Stark 2007, [LIT-2675](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2675.md). It corroborates [CLAIM-709](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-709.md). | Active — read in full 2026-11-17 ([NOTE-2061](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2061.md)) from the Vermont Legislature's committee records, as the read neighbour of Stark (2007), [LIT-2675](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2675.md), which could not be read; worth reading here as Stark's own short statement of the book's thesis: partner abuse as a strategic course of conduct aimed at liberty, which responses to discrete assaults miss. |
| [LIT-2773](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2773.md) | Global Institutions and Human Rights: A Critical Essay on Thomas Pogge, and the Attribution of Remedial Responsibility in Cases of Human Rights Violations | Jordan Shaw-Young (2008), MA thesis, Queen's University. A critique of Pogge whose chapter on David Miller reports, quoting National Responsibility and Global Justice (2007, pp. 100–104), Miller's separation of outcome from remedial responsibility and his connection theory: remedial responsibility is assigned through "moral responsibility, outcome responsibility, causal responsibility, benefit, capacity, and community". Capacity alone can make a faultless bystander responsible ("if I am the only person walking along a river bank when a child falls in, then it is my responsibility to rescue the child"), and a coerced agent can inherit the duty of repair when the coercer "disappears from the scene". Shaw-Young argues that only moral and outcome responsibility ground duties of justice. Registered as the weak read neighbour of Miller 2001, [LIT-2755](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2755.md). It corroborates the second half of [CLAIM-717](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-717.md). | Active — read in part 2026-11-17 ([NOTE-2064](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2064.md)) from Queen's University's repository, as a weak read neighbour of Miller (2001), [LIT-2755](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2755.md), which could not be read; worth reading here only for its chapter on Miller, which reports with page numbers the connection theory of remedial responsibility as Miller states it in National Responsibility and Global Justice (2007). Read: abstract and thesis pp. 18–29. |
| [LIT-2774](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2774.md) | Against Good Caring? Meeting Immediate and Distant Needs Democratically | Joan C. Tronto (2014). Against Good Caring? Meeting Immediate and Distant Needs Democratically. Slides of a paper given at the University of Humanistic Studies (UvH), Utrecht, 30 January 2014. Opposes "neoliberal care" ("Good care = personal responsibility + market") to democratic caring, defines democracy as "the allocation of caring responsibilities in a political community and the method of giving equal voice to all members of the community in making these allocations", and names two misallocations: excluding those "you want to saddle with the most difficult tasks", and exemption, absenting oneself "because one has more important duties: protection, production, taking care of one's own". | [LIT-2775](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2775.md) | A Sociologist's Perspective on Domestic Violence: A Conversation with Michael Johnson, Ph.D. | Michael P. Johnson, interviewed by Theodora Ooms (CLASP, 2006). Johnson divides intimate partner violence into three types by the control context in which it occurs: situational couple violence ("the most common form"), intimate terrorism (violence "in combination with other control tactics" by a batterer who "takes complete control of his partner") and violent resistance ("when a victim of intimate terrorism fights back"). Agency samples and general surveys reach different types, which is why they disagree about gender. To classify a couple's violence, ask about "power and control issues" and fear. Registered as the read neighbour of Johnson 1995, [LIT-2751](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2751.md), and Johnson 2008, [LIT-2715](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2715.md). It corroborates [CLAIM-709](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-709.md): violence is typed by control context, not by a count of acts. | Active — read in full 2026-11-17 ([NOTE-2066](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2066.md)) as a read neighbour of Johnson (1995), [LIT-2751](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2751.md), and Johnson (2008), [LIT-2715](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2715.md), neither of which could be read; worth reading here as Johnson's own short statement of the three-type typology (situational couple violence, intimate terrorism, violent resistance), typed by control context, and of his account of why agency data and general surveys disagree about gender. |

| [LIT-2782](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2782.md) | 49 U.S. Code § 1154: Discovery and use of cockpit and surface vehicle recordings and transcripts | 49 U.S.C. § 1154 (1994, as amended), read in [NOTE-2081](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2081.md). Subsection (b): "No part of a report of the Board, related to an accident or an investigation of an accident, may be admitted into evidence or used in a civil action for damages resulting from a matter mentioned in the report." The NTSB's regulations confine the bar to the Board's report of its determinations, probable cause included, and not its investigators' factual reports (49 CFR 835.2), and state that investigations "are not conducted for the purpose of determining the rights, liabilities, or blame of any person or entity" (49 CFR 831.4(c)). Cook (1998; Revision D, 2000), "How Complex Systems Fail", read in [NOTE-2083](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2083.md). Eighteen points: catastrophe needs several failures, each insufficient; "no isolation of the 'root cause' of an accident is possible", and evaluation by root cause reflects "the social, cultural need to blame specific, localized forces or events"; "Actions at the sharp end resolve all ambiguity" that organizations leave, "often intentionally"; systems run "because people can make it function, despite the presence of many flaws", and outsiders see that work only after accidents. It corroborates [CLAIM-707](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-707.md) and [CLAIM-702](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-702.md) and bears on [QUESTION-476](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-476.md) ([THEORY-1998](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1998.md)). | Active — read 2026-11-18 in full ([NOTE-2083](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2083.md)) from the PDF on Adaptive Capacity Labs' site, Cook's own firm, Revision D (00.04.21); worth reading as the short statement of the safety-science view behind blameless review: failure has many contributors, "root cause" answers a social need to blame, and the sharp end resolves the ambiguity the organization leaves. Nyce (2013), "Just culture: "Evidence", power and algorithms", Journal of Hospital Administration 2(3): 73–77, read in [NOTE-2080](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-2080.md). Algorithms that sort error into human error, at-risk and reckless behaviour treat culpability as an objective fact, but whether a response is just "depends on where one is located in the organization and medical competence hierarchy, and who gets to say"; a survey they relay found accountability rated worst and the most powerful group most satisfied. Worth reading here as an argued critique of just culture in practice: a response to error that one group finds just, others find unjust, and the difference tracks power, so a no-blame or just-culture scheme can carry blame along the hierarchy.
